name: Rafael Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Rafael. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Does that sound all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yeah, of course. I'm curious what other people say, actually.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior at Harwood Electrical, a contractor that wires new-build estates on the edge of town. Right now we're on a site with 120 houses, and I do first fix, which means running all the cables before the plasterers come, then second fix, putting on the sockets and switches. I use an AI app every day to look up regs and check cable runs, and I watch videos at night to get faster. I like the pace and the lads, but the cold and the mud on site in winter are grim.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Bit of a let-down, but okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was overhyped but the tools are still handy, which is what I already think. I'd post a video of how I use AI to check my cable runs, for the other juniors. I'd be the guy saying it's still worth learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my real worry is housing, not AI. Nobody on a housing estate is worried about AI. Everyone on a housing estate is worried about whether the developer starts the next phase of houses. Phase three on our site is on hold because sales are slow, and I've got about 200 saved after buying a new tester.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI to learn the regs faster so I can pass my licence early. I'd keep doing smart-home set-ups at weekends, doorbells and thermostats, for about 40 a job. I'd ask Harwood whether they'd move me to the repair team if new-builds slow down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I like where my skills are going, but I don't like my bank balance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you do with the weekend money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly it pays my share of the bills in a house with two flatmates. The rest went on tools. I'd like it to go into savings, but I keep spending it on gear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If phase three stays on hold, what happens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Harwood would move some of us to another site an hour away or cut hours. Juniors go first, always. I'd probably try to get onto the repair and maintenance side, which is steadier.

say: I'd say AI was **overhyped** but still handy.
I'd post videos showing **other juniors** how I use it.
think: My real worry is **housing sales**, not AI.
Phase three is **on hold**, and I've got about **200** saved.
do: Use AI to learn the regs and pass my **licence early**.
Do **smart-home set-ups** at weekends for about 40 a job.
Ask Harwood about moving to the **repair team**.
feel: Uneasy: good about my skills, worried about my **bank balance**.

fieldNote: His job hangs on the **housing market**, not technology.

He spends side income on **tools**, not savings.

steps.text: Use the AI app nightly to revise regs for the licence
Do weekend doorbell and thermostat set-ups for 40 a job
Ask Harwood about a move to the repair team

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking tasks go first. That's mostly the office side for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big chance for people who learn the tools. I'd say on the site group chat that juniors should start using AI now. I'd say the office lads should get ahead of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it helps me. I use AI to learn faster, not to work less. A junior who learns in two years what used to take five is worth keeping. The site office would shrink, but someone still has to put cable in walls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay for an online course on smart-home controls, about 150 over three months. I'd buy a second-hand thermal camera to find faults faster on my weekend jobs. I'd ask the foreman to let me plan cable runs with the AI tool for the next phase.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly excited. A bit nervous about money, as always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd spend 150 on a course with 200 saved. Is that risky?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, it is, but it'd pay for itself in a few weekend jobs. I've never been good at saving. I'd rather put money into skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the site would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pete, who does the scheduling and orders in the site office. He's 55 and hates computers. If the software does his job, I don't know where he goes.

I'd tell juniors on the site chat to **start using AI** now.
think: A junior who **learns faster** is worth keeping.
The **site office** would shrink, but someone still puts cable in walls.
do: Pay **150** for an online smart-home controls course.
Buy a second-hand **thermal camera** for weekend fault-finding.

fieldNote: He sees thinking AI as a way to **learn faster** and stand out.
He spends scarce money on **skills and tools** rather than a cushion.
He worries for Pete, an older **office worker**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2028, then robots in 2031. That's quick for new-build.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is huge and people need to move now. I'd post about it a lot, telling juniors to learn controls and commissioning. I'd say the government should help with training, because not everyone can pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think new-build wiring is one of the first hands-on jobs to go. First fix on a new-build is the same 40 houses wired the same way. If I were building a robot, that's exactly the job I'd teach it first. I'd be 31 with no licence and no savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to move from first fix to commissioning and fault-finding, starting now. I'd stop buying tools and save 50 a week. I'd apply to the company that services the estates' heating and ventilation systems after people move in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'm excited by the tech and scared for my job at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said not everyone can pay for training. Can you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. I'd do what I can online, but the proper courses are a few thousand. I'd need an employer to sponsor me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes in your day in 2028, before the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The planning, the cable schedules and the ordering would all be AI. I'd get the drawings already worked out and just wire them. That makes me even more like a robot for three years, which isn't great.

I'd call for **government help** with training costs.
think: New-build first fix is the **first hands-on job** robots would learn.
I'd be **31** with no licence and no savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Robots 2034. That's better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough if you start this year. I'd post a plan: licence, then controls, then commissioning. I'd tell juniors not to wait for their bosses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel I could get ahead. Five years is enough to move from pulling cable on new-builds to setting up the control systems in them. Robots will need someone to tell them what's wired where. The houses still need people who understand the systems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get my licence by 2027, then do a building controls course with sponsorship from Harwood if I can. I'd grow the weekend smart-home work and charge more once licensed. I'd save 30 a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a good, busy way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would Harwood sponsor you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because they'll need someone who can set up the systems they're installing. If I show them I'm already learning, they'd rather train me than hire someone new. That's the pitch, anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your flatmates say about your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My flatmates would say I'm obsessed. One's a barista, one's at a call centre. Honestly, I'd worry more about the call centre one in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37 when it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the best case, so no excuses. I'd say young electricians should get qualified and specialise. I'd keep posting tips for the other juniors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be fine. Ten years is time to get qualified, get known for smart-home work and own the van before the robots turn up. By then I'd want to run a small business doing smart homes and controls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get my licence, work two years at Harwood, then go self-employed on smart-home and controls work around 2030. I'd buy a used van with a small loan. I'd use AI for quotes and bookings so I don't need an office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly because of money. The plan is good, it's the getting there on junior pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the hardest part of getting there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Saving. I'm bad at it, and the van and insurance would need a few thousand. I'd probably have to move back to my parents' for a year to do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you be worried about robots in 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, but by then I'd want to be the one buying a robot for the boring jobs. If I own the business, the robot works for me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because new-build wiring is so repetitive that it'd go first and I'd have no time to climb out. What would help is employers sponsoring juniors into controls and commissioning. The robots won't come for the old electricians who know every weird house. The robots will come for juniors like me, wiring identical boxes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the housing market. If houses don't sell, it doesn't matter whether a robot or a person wires them.

headlineQuote: The robots won't come for the old electricians who know every weird house. The robots will come for juniors like me, wiring identical boxes.
portrait: Rafael is a **27-year-old junior** wiring new-build estates for a contractor.
He uses AI **every day** to learn and posts tips for other juniors.
His near-term worry is a **paused housing phase** and almost no savings.
Fast AGI **alarms** him because repetitive new-build wiring is an easy robot target.
With time, he plans to move into **controls** and run his own smart-home business.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because repetitive new-build wiring would go first.
whatWouldHelp: **Employer sponsorship** for juniors to train in controls and commissioning.
